title: Senior's toolkit: changing data you cannot afford to lose
summary: The transaction habit, RETURNING, upserts, batched deletes and safe read-modify-write, with the dialect spellings.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: changing data you cannot afford to lose
steps.body: Every engineer who has fixed data in production by hand has a story about a missing WHERE. Seniors follow the same small ritual every time, so a mistake costs one ROLLBACK instead of a restore from backup.

toolkit.what: Run every manual UPDATE or DELETE inside a transaction. Check the row count and the result, then COMMIT, or ROLLBACK and nothing happened.
flags: make it permanent; only after you checked

toolkit.what: Write the WHERE as a SELECT first, see how many rows and which ones, then change only the first line into UPDATE or DELETE.
flags: look at a sample of them
toolkit.example:
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM shelters WHERE closed_at IS NULL AND region = 'north';
UPDATE shelters SET closed_at = '2026-03-04T02:00:00Z' WHERE closed_at IS NULL AND region = 'north';

toolkit.what: Get back the rows a statement changed, in the same round trip (PostgreSQL, SQLite 3.35+). SQL Server spells it `OUTPUT inserted.id, inserted.stock`.
flags: every column of each changed row
the generated key without a second query
a record of what you removed
toolkit.example: UPDATE stock SET qty = qty - 1 WHERE sku = 'A1' AND qty > 0 RETURNING sku, qty;

toolkit.what: Insert, or update the existing row if the key is taken: an upsert (PostgreSQL, SQLite). SQL Server uses `MERGE`; MySQL uses `ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE`.
flags: the unique column(s) that decide a clash
the value you tried to insert
toolkit.example:
INSERT INTO stock (sku, qty) VALUES ('A1', 5)
ON CONFLICT (sku) DO UPDATE SET qty = stock.qty + excluded.qty;

toolkit.cmd: UPDATE ... SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE stock > 0
toolkit.what: An atomic read-modify-write: the check and the change happen in one statement, so two requests cannot both sell the last item. Check the affected row count: 0 means sold out.
flags: change relative to the current value, not a value read earlier
the business rule, enforced at write time
PostgreSQL/MySQL: lock rows you read when the logic needs several statements

toolkit.cmd: DELETE ... WHERE id IN (SELECT id ... LIMIT 5000)
toolkit.what: Delete or update millions of rows in batches. One giant statement holds locks for minutes and bloats the log; small batches let other work through. Repeat until it affects 0 rows.
flags: batch size; tune so each batch takes well under a second
a loop in a script or job
toolkit.example:
DELETE FROM events
WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM events WHERE created_at < '2025-01-01' LIMIT 5000);

steps.prompt: In psql you typed `BEGIN;` and then the line below, meaning to change one customer. psql prints `UPDATE 48213`. What do you type next?
options: `ROLLBACK;`, then rewrite it with the `WHERE id = ...` you forgot, and check the count says 1
`COMMIT;` and restore the emails from last night's backup
Close psql: the change is not saved yet
`UPDATE customers SET email = email;` to undo it
steps.explain: Inside a transaction nothing is visible to others until COMMIT, and ROLLBACK undoes it all. (Closing psql would also roll back, but say what you mean.) Without the BEGIN, the 48,213 changes would already be permanent.

steps.prompt: Put the steps of a safe manual fix in order.
lines: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE status = 'stuck' AND placed_at < '2026-03-01';
UPDATE orders SET status = 'cancelled' WHERE status = 'stuck' AND placed_at < '2026-03-01' RETURNING id;
-- check: the UPDATE count matches the SELECT count, and the ids look right

steps.prompt: Add 5 to the stock of `A1`, inserting the row if it does not exist yet.
code: ON CONFLICT (sku) DO __1__ SET qty = stock.qty + __2__.qty;
steps.explain: `excluded` is the row you tried to insert. `inserted` is SQL Server's name in `OUTPUT` and triggers, not valid here.

steps.prompt: Two web servers handle "buy the last ticket" at the same moment. Each runs `SELECT seats_left` (gets 1), checks it is above 0, then runs `UPDATE shows SET seats_left = 0`. Two tickets are sold. Which change fixes it with the least code?
options: One statement: `UPDATE shows SET seats_left = seats_left - 1 WHERE id = 9 AND seats_left > 0`, and treat 0 affected rows as sold out
Wrap the SELECT and UPDATE in a transaction at the default isolation level
Retry the UPDATE if it fails
steps.explain: The read and the write were separate, so both saw 1. At the default READ COMMITTED level a transaction alone does not stop that in PostgreSQL or SQL Server. The conditional update checks and changes atomically; `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` is the alternative when the logic needs several steps.

steps.prompt: Match each spelling to its engine.
pairs: PostgreSQL and SQLite: return the changed rows
SQL Server: return the changed rows

steps.title: Make it a habit
steps.body: Never run a manual UPDATE or DELETE outside `BEGIN`, and always run the SELECT with the same WHERE first. In application code, put business rules into the WHERE of the write itself, and check the affected row count.
